title: Bosveld Citrus grower system: first consultation

segments.text: Morning, everyone. Thank you for having me, and thanks for the coffee, Johan. Um, before we start, there's one thing I need to check with all of you. I'd like to keep a transcript of this meeting so I can write up the requirements properly afterwards. And I use an AI assistant that runs on my own laptop to help me sort through the transcript.
Nothing goes to an outside service. Are you all comfortable with that?
Ja, that's fine with
me. Yes, no problem.
Fine, buy me. As long as it doesn't. Ah, end up on the internet somewhere. It

won't. It stays on this laptop, and if anyone wants me to stop at any point, just say so. Okay. How was the road this morning, by the way? I came in on the R71 from Poliquane, and the stop-and-go at the pass was terrible.
Ag, those road works. They've been there since Easter. My wife says they're building a new road, one spade at a time.
It's worse in the

afternoon. The drugs. I'll leave early then. Okay, so I've read the email you sent, Johan, but I'd really like to hear it from you in your own words. Maybe start with the co-op itself, and then what made you pick up the phone?

Sure. So, Barsfeld Citrus Cooperative. We're in Lettsidl, about 25 kilometers outside Tizanine. We pack citrus for our members, mostly oranges, valentias, and navels, then some lemons, and a fair amount of soft citrus, the mandarins. The co-op was started in 1978 by 11 farmers.

And today we've got, uh, about 140 member growers. Some of them are big commercial farms with a few hundred hectares, and some are small growers from the Nkau Nkaua side with five or six hectares. Everybody's fruit comes through the one pack house here, behind this office.
And the pack house runs all year. No,

no. The season is, roughly, from the end of March with the early mandarins until about the middle of September, when the last valentias go through. Outside of that we do maintenance, we do the books, and we argue about prices.
Mostly we argue about prices.

Yeah, mostly. So what made me pick up the phone? Honestly, it's the growers. They phone us all day. Where's my fruit? What was my pack out? When do I get paid? Why did my bins get downgraded? And we can't answer them quickly, because the information is in, I'd say, five different places.
And some of it is on paper.
Five different places. Can you walk me through them?
Precious can do that better than me. She lives in the pack house.
Yeah, okay. So it starts at the Weybridge. A grower's

truck comes in, or a contractor's truck with bins on the back. Each bin is about 400 kilos when it's full. Okay. The truck goes over the Weybridge, and our clerk writes a delivery ticket. It's a carbon book, three copies.

White copy for the grower, pink for the office, yellow stays in the book. Handwritten Handwritten The Weybridge has a little computer with the scale program on it. It's called Weymate, and it prints the weight on a slip. Then the clerk copies the weight onto the ticket, with the grower number, the farm,
the orchard block, the cultivar, and the number of bins. So the weight comes from the machine, but everything else is written by hand. Exactly. Then the bins go into the holding

area. They get a, uh, a cardboard tag tied on with the ticket number, and they wait for the line. It depends. In the peak, sometimes two days. The early mandarins have to go through to greening first, in the rooms at the back, so it can be a while.

The oranges usually go the next day. Ok, and then? Then the bins go onto the line. We've got an optical grader, the optisort, that photographs every fruit and sorts it into classes. Class one for export, class two for the local market, and then juice.
The grader's computer makes a report for each batch. A batch is basically one delivery ticket. Right. And the report says how many cartons of each class and the percentages.
That's what we call the pack-out. And the report, lives on the grader's computer. It lives on the grader's computer. Tani Mariachi in the office
prints them out every afternoon and files them, and then she types the totals into a spreadsheet.
My spreadsheet. Well, it's the co-op's spreadsheet, but I built it.
Ok, so Sifo, the spreadsheet is yours. What does it do?

So the spreadsheet is, ah, the heart of the whole thing, unfortunately. Every delivery is a row. Mariachi types in the ticket from the pink copy, and then she adds the pack-out from the grader report. And then at the end of each month, I use that to work out the advance payments to the growers.
Advance payments meaning?

So in citrus, you don't get paid the full price when you deliver. The fruit gets exported. It goes on a ship. It gets sold in Raderdam or wherever. And only months later do we know the final price. So we pay the growers an advance. So much per carton of class 1. So much per carton of class 2.
A few rand per bin of juice. MMHM. And then after the season, there's a final pool payment, when all the money is in.
Right. So the monthly calculation is the advance, and the pool payment is once a year.
Once a year. Usually in February. And that one's a beast.
I can imagine. And the growers. How do they find out what they've been paid, and why?

They get a statement. I make it in the spreadsheet. And Mariachi prints it and posts it, or emails it to those who have email. Some of them still come and collected at the office. They like to have a cup of tea with her.
How long after the month ends do they get it?
Um, honestly, three weeks. Sometimes more. Because everything has to be typed first and checked, and then I have to reconcile with the bank.
And that's when the phone starts ringing.
So the growers are phoning, because they don't know where they stand for three, four weeks.

Exactly. And look, I understand them. A small grower with six hectares. That's his whole income for the year. Yes. He delivered 30 bins two weeks ago, and he doesn't know whether they packed out at 80% or 40%. Of course, he's going to phone.
How many calls are we
talking about? In the season. I'd say, uh, Mariachi gets 40, 50 calls

a day. And I get the ones about the grading, maybe 10 a day. Those are the angry ones. Why angry? Because when a batch packs out badly, the grower thinks we made a mistake. He thinks his bins got mixed up with someone else's. And sometimes, to be honest, they did.
Because the cardboard tag fell off, or the ticket
number was written badly, and someone read a 7 as a 1. Okay, that's important. How often does that happen? Not often. Maybe, I don't know, two or three times a week in the peak.
But every time it happens, it's a big fight, and it takes a day to sort out. I have to go through the grader reports and the tickets

and phone the driver. Let me make sure I've got the picture. A truck comes in. It goes over the weighbridge. The clerk writes a ticket by hand with the wait from weighmate. The bins get a cardboard tag. They wait. They go through the optisort grader. The grader report gets printed.
Mariat G types the ticket and the packout into Sifo's spreadsheet. And Sifo works out the advance at the end of the month and makes a statement.
That's it. That's the whole sad story. And
the fifth place. Johan said five. Oh,

the QC lab. Sorry. Before a grower picks an orchard, our lab tests samples. The sugar and the acid and the juice percentage to see if the fruit is mature enough for export. Maturity tests. That's on paper too. And the results go to the grower by WhatsApp. Our QC lady takes a photo of the sheet and sends
it. Okay. And spray records. You mentioned export. Yeah,

that's a sixth place now that you mention it. Every grower has to give us his spray records before we can pack his fruit for export because the European buyers test for residues. Those are in a lever arch file in my office. So
there's paper and spreadsheets everywhere and the growers can't see any of it themselves. That's really helpful. What's the most painful
part for you if you had to pick one? The phone
calls. No, wait. The statements. Because if the statements came out in a week, half the phone
calls would go away. For

me, it's the typing. Maraichi types for, what, three, four hours a day in the season. And she's retiring. When? End of June next year. Right in the middle of the season, which is a whole other problem. That's
a real risk. Is there someone to take over from her? Not
yet. We'll advertise. But nobody else knows that spreadsheet like her and Sifo. She knows every grower by name. She knows whose son is farming now and whose wife does the books. Okay.
So let's talk about what you'd like. If this goes well, a year from now, what's different? The growers
can see their own deliveries and their pack out on their phones the same day or the day after. They get their statements in a few days, not three weeks. And we stop answering 50 phone calls a day.
Is there a number you'd want to hit? Fewer calls, faster statements.
Half. If the calls go down by half, I'd be happy. And statements within, let's say, five working days after the month end. Five
working days is tight, but yeah. If I don't have to wait for the typing, it's passable. Good.
I'll write those down as the goals. Precious from the Packhouse side.
Do the bins have
anything on them today? A numbers. The bins belong to the growers, mostly. Some have
numbers painted on, some don't. The co-op has about, uh, 3,000 of its own bins that we lend out to the small growers.
And those have numbers burnt into the plastic. So putting a permanent label on each bin isn't straightforward. No, that's why I said
barcode or something. Maybe the barcode is on the tag, not on the bin. A plastic tag that you clip on and it comes back to the waybridge. I don't know, you're the expert. I'm

not sure I'm the expert on bins, but I'll look into what other pack houses do. Let me note that as something to work out together. So scanning a tag at intake and again when the bin goes onto the line.
Yes, at the tipper where they tip the bins into the water. That's where we'd scan.
Hi, sorry, sorry. Is this the system meeting? Johan said half past nine, I think. Or I heard half past nine. It
was nine, Ryuan. Come in, sit. Ayesha, this is Ryuan. He does our IT. He's not staff, he's a contractor, but he's here every Wednesday and whenever something breaks. Hi,
Ryuan. Nice to meet you. We've just been through how a delivery goes from the waybridge to the statement, and Precious was talking about scanning bins at the tipper. Not
okay. Joh the scanning. Precious has been on about the scanning for a year. Because
it's needed. No, I
agree, I
agree.
Johan, it's actually a good moment for you. What's the network like? At the waybridge and at the tipper? Uh,
so, the office and the pack house are on fiber. It came in two years ago and it's okay. Yeah.
But the

waybridge is at the gate, about 300 meters from the office, and it's on a wireless link, a point to point. When it rains hard, or when there's load shedding and the battery at the gate runs flat, it drops. The tipper is inside the pack house, so that's fine, the wi-fi in there is decent.
How often does the waybridge drop? In the

season, maybe once a week, for an hour or so. And when the whole area's fiber goes down, which happens, someone digs up a cable next to the R36 or whatever, then everything's off. Last year we had a full day once. So the
waybridge has to keep working without the network. It
has to. We cannot stop trucks at the gate. If a truck waits, the fruit sits in the sun and the next 20 trucks are behind it on the
road.
Okay. So the intake has to work offline and catch up when the link is back. I'll write that as a firm requirement.
Yeah. And to be honest, I can put a bigger battery on the gate. That's not expensive. But the fiber outages I can't fix. Let's talk
about Weymate for a second. Is it something you can get data out of? Weymate

is old. It runs on a Windows PC under the counter at the gate. It writes every weighing to a little database file, and it can export a CSV at the end of the day. And I think the scale indicator is connected to the PC by a serial cable.
So if you wanted the wait live, you could probably read it straight from the indicator, without Weymate at all.
That's useful. And the greater, the OptiSort.

That's the problem one. The OptiSort was bought in 2019 from the supplier overseas through their agent in Cape Town. Its computer is locked down. The reports come out as PDFs. There might be a database underneath, but we don't have the password and the agent says if we touch it, we void the support contract.
So getting the packout out of the grader automatically is uncertain.
Very uncertain. I can ask the agent whether they have an export, a CSV or an API or something. They might want money for it.
Would you mind asking them? That's probably the biggest unknown we've got.
Loyal ask. I'll send them an email this week.
Thank you. And if the answer is no, the fallback is someone typing the totals from the report, which is what Mariet G does now.
Or reading the PDF automatically. Can't a computer read a PDF?

Sometimes, if the PDF has real text in it and the layout never changes, I'd need to see a few. Can someone send me some greater reports from last season? I'll send you some. Good batches and bad ones. Perfect. And on the accounting
side, SIFO, what do you use? We use

Ledger 1 for the books. The payments to the growers go out through the bank in a batch file that I upload to the bank's business banking. The spreadsheet makes the batch file, actually. Well, it makes a list and I copy it into the bank's template. So the
payment calculation is in your spreadsheet and Ledger 1 gets the totals.
The totals, yeah. I journal them in at the end of the month. Would
you want the new system to calculate the advances or do you want to keep that in your spreadsheet for now? Hem,

honestly, keep it in my spreadsheet for now. The rules change every season. The board decides different advance rates for different cultivars and sizes, and I don't want to phone a developer every time the board changes its mind. If the system gives me the deliveries and the packout clean, I'll do the sums.
I
agree. Let's not build the payment engine in the first round.

Okay, so that's a decision. The payment calculation stays in SIFO's spreadsheet for phase 1, and the new system gives him the deliveries and packout as an export he can open in the spreadsheet. And then the statement. Does the statement come from the new system or from the spreadsheet?
Um,

that's a good question. If the advance is worked out in my spreadsheet, the statement has to show the advance. So either I upload the amounts back into the system every month or the statement stays in the spreadsheet. Let's
leave that one open for now. I'll come back with a couple of options. It depends on how much work and upload would be for you each month.
Okay. Can we talk
about the growers' information for a bit? What do you hold about them?

Names, ID numbers for the growers who farm as individuals, company registration numbers for the farms that are companies, VAT numbers, bank account details, physical addresses, phone numbers, email, and their delivery history, their packouts, and what they've been paid.
Okay. So for the small growers who farm in their own name, that's all personal information under Popia, and the bank details need care in any case. Who should be able to see what? A grower

must only see his own stuff. That's the number one thing. If grower can see what grower be got paid, I'll have a war on my hands. Right. Seriously. These people are neighbors. Their kids go to the same school. They sit next to each other in
church. I understand. So each grower sees only their own deliveries, packouts, and statements. And in the office.

Me and Johan see everything. Marietje sees everything except, no, actually she sees everything too. Precious and the clerks need the deliveries and the grading, but not the bank details and not the money.

I don't want to see the money. So the roles are something like this. The office and management see everything. The packhouse staff see deliveries and grading, but not bank details or payments. And growers see their own. Who changes a grower's bank details today? Only
me. And only with a letter
from the bank. Because there's fraud. MMS. Last year, someone phoned pretending to be one of our growers and asked us to change his bank account. Luckily, Marietje knew his voice. That's
exactly the kind of thing to design for. So changing bank details stays a manual, checked process in the office, and a grower can't change them from their phone.
Definitely not.
Good. And the weights. What if someone changes a weight or a bin count after the fact?
That must be recorded. Who changed it and why? Because that's where the fights are.
So an audit trail on every change to a delivery. Who changed it, when, what it was before, and the reason.
Yes. And the grower
should be able to see that it was changed, I think.
Hmm. Maybe not the reason. Sometimes the reason is, you know, the driver counted wrong because he was in a hurry to get to the bottle store.
Okay. Maybe not the
reason.
I'll
note that the grower sees that a delivery was corrected, and whether they also see the reason is still to be decided. Juen, where would all this live? Do you have a preference for hosting?
Not on a server in the office, please. I don't want another thing to look after, and the power here isn't reliable. Some cloud thing is fine. The
board said the data must stay in South Africa. One of our members is a lawyer, and he was very firm about that at the last meeting.
Okay. So hosting in a South African data center. That's a constraint, and it's possible with most of the big providers now. Yeah,
they've got Johannesburg and Cape Town regions.
Exactly. And for the Weybridge, the tablet or PC at the gate would keep its own copy of the day's deliveries and send them up when the link is back. And if
the tablet gets stolen?
Good point. Then it should need a PIN or a login, and it shouldn't hold more than it needs. The day's deliveries and the grower list, not bank details.
Okay, that works for me.
How long do you keep the records now? Tickets and statements.
The orderers say five years for anything financial. The tickets we keep, ah, I think also five years in boxes in the storeroom. The mice eat some of them.
Five years then, for deliveries and statements. And when a grower leaves the co-op.
We keep his records for the five years, for tax, and then, honestly, nobody has ever thrown anything away.

That's common. I'll suggest that the system keeps a leaver's records for five years, and then flags them for deletion, and you decide. Let's talk about the growers themselves. How do they use their phones? What kind of phones?
Everything. The big farmers have iPhones and laptops, and their own farm managers. The small growers, a lot of them have cheap Android phones, and data
is expensive. Some of them, the older ones, their kids do the phone stuff for them.
So whatever the growers use has to work on a cheap Android phone, on a slow connection, without eating their data. Yeah,
and I don't want them to have to download an app. Last time somebody made us an app, for the, uh, the study group, nobody installed it. Twelve people out of a hundred and forty. A web page
they open from a link, then. One they can save to the home screen, like an app.
That's fine. And
SMS. Not everybody uses WhatsApp properly, but everybody gets smsays. What would you send them? When
their batch is graded. Your delivery number 4471, packed out at 78% class one, something like that, with a link to see
the rest. That's
a nice one. Johan, are you happy with SMS? SMS
is fine. WhatsApp costs money if you do it through the business, doesn't it ruin? Yeah, it's
per message through one of the providers. But SMS also costs about, I think, 25, 30 cents a message. Then
let's say SMS for the grading notifications to start with, and maybe WhatsApp later. Are you all okay with that?
Yeah, fine. Good,
that's decided. And how does a grower log in? Most of them won't want another password.
No passwords. They'll forget it and phone us.
One option is a code sent by SMS to the phone number you already have on file for them. They type the code and they are in. That
works if the number on file is right. Some of them change their numbers. Then updating
a phone number would go through the office, like the bank details, so nobody can take over someone else's account by changing the number.
Yeah, same rule. Now
language. The growers speak.
English Afrikaans zitsonga sepedi. Most of the small growers are zitsonga speakers.
My mother would want it in zitsonga, but she reads English too. Do you want the grower pages translated?
Hum, I don't know. It would be nice, but the statements are in English now and nobody complains. The statements have to be in
English for the orderers anyway.
So the minimum is English. Whether we also do zitsonga and maybe Afrikaans for the grower pages, I'll leave open and I'll tell you what it would cost to add.
Yeah, let's see the cost first.
And how should it look? Do you have any preferences? Colors style.
Our colors are orange and dark green. The logo is an orange with a leaf on it. Use that. And big, clear writing. Some of our members are 70, 75.
For the Weybridge
big buttons, the clerk sometimes has gloves on in winter and it's dusty. And it's outside under the roof but
outside, so the screen must be readable in the sun. Would that be a tablet at the Weybridge or the PC? A tablet, I think. A rugged
one. The PC is under the counter and the clerk has to go inside the little office to use it while the driver waits. Then it
needs to be charged every day and with the battery at the gate.
We'll keep it
charged, Ruan.
Okay, okay. I'll

write it down as a strong preference for a rugged tablet at the Weybridge and I'll check the hardware cost. And for the growers, plain and simple, their deliveries, their packout, their statements, and not much else. Not
much else. If it's complicated, they'll phone us to ask how it works, which defeats the whole point. When the truck
leaves, does the driver still need a paper ticket?
Yes. The driver must leave with something in his hand, otherwise the grower phones to ask if the fruit arrived. A small printed
slip is fine, like a till slip. So a small printer next to the tablet, that prints a slip for each grower on the truck. Yes. And the SMS too, if they want it. But the slip always.
The old ones like paper.
And if the tablet itself breaks on a busy morning.
We keep the carbon books in the drawer, just in case. Then someone types them in afterwards.
That's sensible. I'll make sure there's
a quick way to enter the paper tickets afterwards, so nothing gets lost.
Yah, keep the books. Tablets always die at the worst moment.
Okay. Let's talk volumes. How many trucks come through
the Weybridge in a day? In the peak, 60, 70
trucks. Mostly between 6 and 10 in the morning, because they pick in the "No, actually that's not right." They pick in the morning and

they deliver late morning. Between 7 and 11 say. And each truck carries how many bins? It depends on the truck. A small grower's backy with a trailer, 6 bins. A big truck, 40 bins. Does one truck always carry one grower's fruit?
No, and that's another headache. The small

growers around Engkau and Kau share transport. There's a contractor, Mr. Shirinza, with two trucks, and he collects from 6 or 7 growers in one trip. Right. So one truck comes over the Weybridge with 7 grower's bins on it. We weigh the whole truck, and then we have to split the weight by grower, by the number of bins each one has on the truck.
The clerk
does it with a calculator. So one truck can carry several grower's bins, and the weight gets shared out. Is it always by the number of bins? By bins.
We can't weigh each
bin separately, there's no bin scale. So it's the full truck minus the empty truck, divided by the bins, and each grower gets his share.
And the growers accept that.
They accept it because it's always been

like that. Mostly. I'll make sure the intake can split one truck's weight across several growers by their number of bins, and that each grower's ticket shows his own share. Does the contractor need to see anything?
No. The contractor gets paid by the growers directly. That's not our business.
So how many bins in a day at the peak? About 1800 bins a day at the peak. And how
long does a truck take at the Weybridge now? Four, five minutes when it's going well. The riding is
what takes the time. When there's a queue, it backs up onto the road, and then the traffic department
phones Johan.
Twice last season.
What would be good enough for the clerk? Under a minute. If they can scan and tap and go under a minute for the clerk's part.
So capturing a delivery at the Weybridge should take the clerk less than a minute, And it must keep up with 70 trucks in about four hours. Yes. Oh, and
sorry, I said 1800 bins. That's what we do on a normal day in June, July. The peak last season in the big Valencia week was 2400 bins in one day.
2400 at the peak and about 1800 on a normal day in the middle of the season. Thank you. That matters for the sizing.
And it's growing. We've got two new members planting, and the old naval orchards are being replaced with mandarins, which means smaller fruit and more cartons per bin.
Any idea how much growth?
The board's plan says 10% more volume a year for the next five years. Whether that happens with the prices the way they are, I don't know.
I'll design for that anyway. It's not a big number for a system like this. And how many growers would use the portal?
Well, all hundred and forty. Johan, it's a hundred and sixty-two. A hundred and
forty delivered last season, but we have a hundred and sixty-two members. The others haven't delivered for a season or two, but they can come back any time, and they still get the newsletter.
You're okay, a hundred and sixty-two. He's the one with the list. So up to a
hundred and sixty-two growers, and some will have more than one person logging in. A farm manager and the owner, say. The
big farms, yes. The owner and his manager, and maybe his bookkeeper. So a few
hundred users at most. That's small. The bigger load is the morning rush at the Weybridge, and the notifications going out after grading.
And when everybody opens their statement on the same morning.
Yeah, that too. Still small numbers, but the pages should be quick on a slow phone. I'd aim for grower's page loading in, say,
three seconds on a 3G connection.
That's fine. Most of them have 3G at least. Some of the farms up towards the mountain have nothing, but then they come down to town.

Except after the hail. Did you hear Ayasha? Last Saturday, a hailstorm went right over Letzidel. Ten minutes. Some of the farms on the Rubbervale Road lost half the crop on the trees. Oh no. That's terrible. My cousin's farm a whole block of navels all marked.
It's juice now.
It happens every few years. That's farming anyway.
Johan, apart from the growers, what do you need to see as the manager? Day to day.

Every morning I want to know what came in yesterday. How many bins per cultivar and what the packout was. Right now I walk over to Precious and ask her and she looks in her notebook. It's a very good notebook. It's a very good notebook, but when I'm in Johansberg at the citrus meeting, I can't walk over.
So a daily summary for management. Bins received and the packout per cultivar for the day before. On the phone or by email.
Both. An email at six in the morning would be perfect and a page I can look at.
Okay. Any other reports? For the board or for the export agent?
The board wants a monthly report. Volumes, packout, advances paid. I make that by hand too in the spreadsheet and it takes me a day.
That one I'd probably leave in your spreadsheet for the first phase since the advances are there. But the volumes and packout could come straight from the system. Does that sound right? That
sounds right.
Okay. Precious, at the tipper, what happens when a bin is scanned? What would you want to see? The grower, the blark, the
cultivars. And if it's the last bin of that delivery, so the line knows to close the batch on the grader. Right now the line foreman shouts. He shouts. He shouts, last bin 4471.
Okay. And the
grader operator types it in. If he doesn't hear two growers'

fruit go into one batch. MM. So the scan at the tipper should tell the operator when a delivery's last bin has gone in. Yes. That alone would save me half my fights. That's a good one. Can I ask about the clerks? How many people would use the Weybridge and tipper screens?
Two clerks at the
Weybridge, one in the morning shift,
one in the afternoon, and in the peak both together. And at
the tipper, three people over the shifts. Plus me, plus the foreman. And how comfortable are they with computers? The Weybridge clerks okay. They use WhatsApp,
they use the Weymate screen. The tipper guys less. They'll want one butter.
One butter. I like that. Before we get to money, have you looked at buying a packhouse system off the shelf?

We did three years ago. There's a big one that the large packhouses use from Cape Town. They wanted, I think, two million rand plus a yearly license, and it does a hundred things we don't need. For a co-op our size, it doesn't make sense.
And it didn't have the small grower stuff, the sharing of trucks, the SMS.
That's helpful to know. So buying the big system was ruled out, mainly on cost.
On cost, and because the people who sold it never came back to us after the demo.
Okay. Can we talk about budget? Do you have a figure in mind?
The board approved, uh, 650,000 rand for the system. That was at the August meeting.

I'm not sure that's right, Johan. I think it was less. Was it, uh, I remember 650. 650 was what Ruan's friend quoted us last year for the app thing. The board approved something lower. Let me grab the resolution. One sec. It's in the file on my desk.
There
he is. Did you find it?

Yeah. Okay. Sorry about that. Here it is. Resolution of the 21st of August. Okay. The board approves an amount of up to 580,000 rand, excluding VAT, for the development of a grower information system and running costs of up to 4,500 rand per month.
So it's 580, not 650.
580. Okay. I stand corrected.
Thank you, Sifo. It's helpful to have it exactly. 580,000, excluding VAT for the build, and up to 4,500 a month to run it. Does the 4,500 include the SM says?
It doesn't say, "Hum, I'd assume so. Everything it takes to run it."
Then I'll assume it includes the SM says and the hosting, and I'll show you the monthly breakdown so you can check it against the resolution. Is the build amount for this financial year?
Our year ends in February, so whatever we spend before the end of February comes from this year's budget. After that, it would have to go to the board again.
Okay. That's good to know. That probably means paying in stages, with most of it before the end of February.
Yeah, that would suit us. And the
